q: The central idea of the passage is that discipline:
passage:
Passage 1 - Discipline and Performance
Discipline is often misunderstood as mere obedience to rules. In demanding institutions, however, it has a wider meaning. It includes the ability to control impulses, keep commitments, manage time, and continue working even when motivation is low. A disciplined person does not depend entirely on mood. He or she builds routines that make useful action easier and harmful delay less likely. Discipline therefore supports reliability: teammates can predict that a disciplined person will prepare, arrive on time, and complete assigned duties. Yet discipline without judgment can become mechanical. Mature discipline combines consistency with the ability to adapt when circumstances genuinely change.
expl: The passage broadens discipline beyond obedience and includes judgment.

q: The passage argues that errors become useful when learners:
passage:
Passage 2 - Learning from Error
Errors are unavoidable in serious learning. Their value, however, depends on what happens after they are noticed. Repeating an error without analysis produces little improvement. Effective learners identify the cause, correct the method, and test the correction under similar conditions. They also distinguish between a careless mistake and a conceptual misunderstanding. The first may require better attention; the second may require rebuilding knowledge from the foundation. This process can feel slower than simply doing more questions, but it usually produces more durable progress because it changes the mechanism that caused the failure.
expl: The key idea is analysis, correction, and retesting.

q: According to the passage, pressure can:
options: narrow attention and cause information to be overlooked
passage:
Passage 3 - Decision Making Under Pressure
Pressure narrows attention. This can be useful when a task demands immediate focus, but it can also make a person overlook information that would normally be considered. Good decision makers therefore use simple structures under stress: they identify the objective, separate facts from assumptions, compare the most realistic options, and consider the likely consequences of each. They also know when time is too limited for perfect information. In such cases, the goal is not certainty but a reasonable decision based on the best available evidence. Afterward, reviewing the outcome helps improve future judgment.
expl: The passage presents both a benefit and a risk of narrowed attention.

q: The passage says individual talent alone is:
options: not sufficient for effective team performance
passage:
Passage 4 - Teamwork
A team is not effective merely because its members are individually talented. Performance depends on coordination: members must understand the objective, know their responsibilities, share relevant information, and adjust when another member encounters difficulty. Trust reduces the time spent checking whether others will perform basic duties, but trust does not mean the absence of accountability. Strong teams make standards clear and address problems early. They also avoid confusing agreement with unity. Members may disagree about methods while still remaining committed to the same mission.
expl: Coordination is presented as essential beyond individual talent.

q: Efficient readers vary their pace according to:
passage:
Passage 5 - Reading Efficiently
Efficient reading is not the same as reading every line at maximum speed. Skilled readers vary their pace according to purpose. They may scan a page to locate a date, skim an article to grasp its main argument, or read slowly when a paragraph contains dense reasoning. They also monitor comprehension. If a key sentence is unclear, they pause, reread, and connect it with surrounding ideas. This flexible approach is especially useful in timed tests, where spending too long on one difficult sentence can reduce the time available for easier questions.
expl: The passage states that pace depends on purpose.
